newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: ILO seeks to spur discussion on child labour.
newsitem.headline: ILO seeks to spur discussion on child labour.

text.p: International experts begin a two-day conference in Amsterdam on Wednesday to consider how to eradicate the most exploitative forms of child labour such as child prostitution, debt bondage and slavery.

The International Labour Organisation (ILO), which is co-hosting the conference with the Dutch government, estimates that more than 250 million children around the world are working full-time, many under extremely hazardous conditions.
Their plight will be discussed in Amsterdam by some 200 government ministers, labour union leaders, officials of employer organisations and representatives of working children.
The United Nations Children's Fund (Unicef) says most, but by no means all, working children live in developing countries.
In India alone, Labour Ministry officials say some 18 million children are at work rather than at school, while children's rights activists put the figure at around 55 million.
Unicef estimates that in Africa one child in three works and in Latin America one in five.
Several affected countries have recently been stirred to action by growing international outrage.
In December, India said it had taken 150,000 child labourers out of hazardous industries under a plan to eliminate children from such jobs by 2002.
Bangladesh's garment industry, faced with U.S. import restrictions, now also says it is free of child labour.
And on February 14, the ILO, child welfare advocates and sporting goods manufacturers announced a plan to end the use of child labour in making soccer balls in Pakistan.
Concerted action on child labour has been complicated by the political dimension of the debate.
Developing nations are suspicious of Western interference in the area of workers' rights, fearing this will undermine their main advantage in world trade -- cheap labour.
Some contend Western nations are using the issue to disguise nascent protectionism and to gain unfair trade advantages.
Nonetheless, developing countries will be well represented in Amsterdam, with the Labour ministers of India, Bangladesh, Brazil, Thailand, Tanzania and Egypt all due to attend.

Working children's organisations themselves are also often divided on how underage workers should be viewed. Some grassroots unions and associations support calls for an end to all forms of child labour.

But others defend poor childrens' right to work to help support their families and concentrate their efforts on gaining traditional labour benefits, such as better pay and conditions, for their members.
Working children from several countries are being brought to the conference to contribute their views and experiences.

At a meeting on Monday night, some were clear about their distrust of recent international efforts like boycotts of industries known to employ child labour, saying they wanted recognition as children, but also as organised workers.
"If you prevent children from working honestly all you will do is push them on to the streets to become criminals," one young delegate said.
But Basrur Lakshmi, a domestic servant from the age of eight and now, at 17, an organiser for an Indian working childrens' union, said the conference marked an important step.
"This is the very first time we have been invited to take part in decision-making affecting our own lives," she said.
